newArtifact.identityNotesMd: No `/StructureDefinition-Media.json` file exists in the R6 package, and the R6 `.index.json` has no `StructureDefinition` entry with id, type, url, or filename corresponding to `Media`. Searches also found no R6 `Media` resource instances or direct `StructureDefinition/Media` references. narrativeReportMd:
# Media R4->R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
`Media` is a hard breaking removal in the supplied R6 ballot4 core package: R4 instances with `resourceType: "Media"` have no same-named R6 StructureDefinition and will not validate as an R6 core resource. This is a critical R4-to-R6 instance, API, search, and code-generation break.

## Scope
The assigned artifact was R4 `Media`. The R6 package was checked for an exact `Media` StructureDefinition and for likely renamed artifacts. No direct successor was found. `DocumentReference`, `ImagingSelection`, and `DiagnosticReport.media.link` were inspected as migration context only.

## Main migration themes
The main migration task is not a simple element rename. Implementers must choose a target representation, most commonly `DocumentReference` for externally referenced or inline document-like media, `ImagingSelection`/`ImagingStudy` for DICOM imaging selection context, or resource-specific references such as R6 `DiagnosticReport.media.link` to `DocumentReference`. Several R4 `Media` fields have partial or semantic mappings but no guaranteed lossless home.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest impact is the resource identity removal itself (`Media:ARTIFACT_IDENTITY:root:0f4f86`). A secondary high-impact runtime issue is that generated classes, `resourceType` dispatch, REST endpoints, and Media-specific search parameters disappear as R6 core surfaces (`Media:SERIALIZATION_OR_CODEGEN:Media:5d8c2b`). The most important manual-review areas are lifecycle status mapping, content mapping, and preservation of acquisition/technical metadata.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is needed to choose target resources and map semantics: R4 event-status values do not align cleanly with `DocumentReference.status`/`docStatus` or `ImagingSelection.status`; R4 dimensions, duration, view, device name, and device references may require extensions or DICOM-oriented resources; and R4 media terminology is not present as R6 media-specific terminology.

## Backward-compatible design observations
A less disruptive design would have kept `Media` as deprecated or retained a compatibility profile/StructureMap. The supplied computable package does not include rationale, so this report cannot judge whether removal was necessary, only that it is materially breaking.

## Follow-up analysis
Review the R6 `DocumentReference`, `ImagingSelection`, `ImagingStudy`, and `DiagnosticReport` reports together with any official cross-version mapping once available.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `Media` is absent from the supplied R6 ballot4 package, so R4 `Media` instances are not valid R6 core instances. Top migration concerns are selecting a replacement resource, preserving lifecycle/status semantics, and retaining media-specific acquisition metadata. The largest uncertainty is the lack of an official R4 Media -> R6 migration map.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is a representational redesign. Raw R4 `Media` cannot be version-bumped; systems must transform to another R6 resource pattern. `DocumentReference` can carry the attachment and many document-like metadata fields, `ImagingSelection` can carry selected DICOM instance context, and R6 `DiagnosticReport.media.link` points to `DocumentReference` rather than `Media`. These candidate targets differ in required status codes, subject/performer targets, cardinalities, and terminology.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high that the `Media` resource itself is removed because both the expected file path and the R6 package index lack a `Media` StructureDefinition. Confidence is medium for specific migration recommendations because the local inputs do not include official change notes, narrative migration guidance, terminology expansions, or an authoritative conversion map.

findings.title: R6 core package has no Media resource StructureDefinition

oldState.summary: R4 defines `Media` as a concrete resource.

semanticText.definition: A photo, video, or audio recording acquired or used in healthcare. The actual content may be inline or provided by direct reference.

oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 package contains `StructureDefinition-Media.json` with canonical `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/Media`, kind `resource`, type `Media`, derivation `specialization`, and `abstract: false`.

newState.narrativeMd: The expected R6 file path is absent and the R6 package index has no `StructureDefinition` with id, type, url, or filename for `Media`. No same-named resource can validate an instance with `resourceType: "Media"`.

facts.note: The R6 assigned path does not exist.

facts.oldValue: Media is a valid R4 resource type
facts.newValue: Media is not defined as an R6 core resource type in the supplied package

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The comparison is an identity check rather than a fuzzy element match. The old canonical has no same-canonical or same-name R6 StructureDefinition in the local package.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation break. A syntactically valid R4 `Media` instance cannot be an R6 core instance because the resource type is not defined. Runtime dispatch, validation, persistence schemas, REST endpoints, subscriptions, and FHIRPath/resource-type switches that expect `Media` require redesign.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Clinical images, audio, video, scanned documents, and biometric media can be clinically or operationally important. The main risk is data loss or misclassification during migration rather than an unsafe interpretation of a single changed field.

justification.inferredGoal: Retire the standalone trial-use Media resource and use other resources such as DocumentReference and imaging-specific resources for media content and references.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain Media in R6 as a deprecated base resource while steering new implementations to DocumentReference and imaging resources.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Retiring a draft, generic `Media` resource in favor of document and imaging-specific resources is a reasonable R6 goal. A deprecated R6 `Media` resource would have avoided the hard validation break for existing data, but it would materially undercut consolidation by leaving two core ways to represent the same media content. With no official rationale in the local inputs, the removal is not proven necessary, but the duplicate-representation and maintenance costs make the break probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would have kept `Media` in the R6 core package as deprecated, with definitions pointing to preferred replacement resources. That would preserve most R4-valid instances. The tradeoff is substantial: core packages, validators, servers, search parameters, generated SDKs, and interoperability guidance would need to support a legacy resource alongside `DocumentReference` and imaging resources indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances, but keeps duplicate resource, API, search, validation, and codegen surfaces that may never disappear.

evidence.detail: R4 defines a concrete resource StructureDefinition for Media.
The expected R6 StructureDefinition file is absent.
No R6 package index entry identifies a Media StructureDefinition.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows the minimal shape relevant to the break: `Media.status` is required in R4 and `Media.content` is required. In R6 core, the `resourceType` itself has no definition.

findings.narrativeMd: `Media` disappears as a core resource in the supplied R6 package. This is not a normal element-level tightening where an instance can be repaired by adding a field; the root `resourceType` is no longer recognized. Any R4 data store, API, validator, or generated model that stores `Media` resources needs a migration target before it can claim R6 conformance.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid `Media` instance becomes R6-invalid because no R6 `StructureDefinition/Media` exists. This affects strict parsers, validators, JSON schema generation, FHIRPath type checks, REST route tables, compartment/search configuration, and resource-type enums. There is no R6 `Media` content to round-trip back to R4; round-trip questions instead apply to whichever replacement resources are selected.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all persisted and exchanged `Media` resources. Decide whether each use case should become `DocumentReference`, `ImagingSelection`/`ImagingStudy`, an `Observation`/`DiagnosticReport` attachment pattern, or an implementation-specific extension/profile. Do not only change `resourceType`; map lifecycle, subject, performer/operator, encounter/context, body site, attachment, and technical metadata explicitly.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The break could have been avoided for existing data by retaining `Media` as deprecated. If the goal was to consolidate document-like media under `DocumentReference`, an R6 compatibility period with canonical maps would have reduced disruption. Without the official rationale, this report cannot determine whether the cleanup benefit outweighed the migration cost.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `Media` is a concrete resource and the R6 ballot4 package has no `Media` StructureDefinition or index entry. That makes existing `resourceType: Media` instances invalid as R6 core resources, not merely in need of an element-level repair. R6 `DocumentReference` explicitly says it can cover photos, video, and audio, so consolidation has a plausible goal, but whole-resource removal still deserves renewed transition scrutiny because it changes resource identity, storage partitions, endpoint contracts, and validation. A lightweight public search found multiple public IG/profile repositories using `Media` profiles, which is not proof of broad deployment but is enough to keep the low-FMM break from being dismissed as purely theoretical.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-Media.json: concrete resource, url http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/Media, type Media, abstract false.
R6 package: StructureDefinition-Media.json is absent and the R6 .index.json query returned no Media StructureDefinition or Media search entries.
R6 DocumentReference definition says a document includes photo, video, or audio recordings acquired or used in healthcare.

GitHub code search for public `Parent: Media` FSH profiles returned examples such as JP_Media_Endoscopy, IL-Core-Media, and pathology imaging profiles; this suggests IG-level relevance but not confirmed production prevalence.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 Media is FMM 1 and trial-use, so removal is not judged with normative-level stability expectations. The top-level old-valid/new-invalid break and public IG-profile evidence nevertheless make the transition concern material.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: an R4 instance whose root resourceType is Media has no corresponding R6 core resource definition.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could have retained `Media` as deprecated for one major release, possibly with preferred mappings to `DocumentReference` and imaging resources. That would preserve old instances and validators, but it would keep a duplicate resource, REST endpoint, search family, and codegen surface alive while R6 tries to consolidate media under other resources.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report correctly treats this as a hard top-level break and its Partial deprecated-resource alternative is plausible, but the Critical framing should be tempered by FMM 1/trial-use status rather than treated like mature or normative content.

findings.title: Media-specific serialization, generated models, REST routes, and search surface are removed

oldState.summary: R4 provides a first-class `Media` resource type with Media-specific elements and search parameters.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 package index includes `StructureDefinition-Media.json` and resource-specific search parameters such as `Media-status`, `Media-identifier`, `Media-subject`, `Media-type`, `Media-modality`, `Media-created`, and `Media-device`.

newState.summary: R6 has no first-class `Media` model or Media-specific search parameter family in the supplied package.
newState.narrativeMd: Because there is no R6 `Media` StructureDefinition, generated R6 SDKs and validators built from this package should not generate a `Media` class, `Media` enum member, or `/Media` endpoint from core definitions.

facts.note: The JSON `resourceType` literal has no R6 core StructureDefinition target.
The R6 index search for Media-specific definitions found no corresponding `Media-*` search parameters.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is the runtime/codegen face of the same resource removal. The validation break is counted in the artifact-identity finding; separately, generated code and operational APIs that compile or route against `Media` will fail or need compatibility shims.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Operational workflows that retrieve diagnostic images or media by Media-specific search parameters can silently lose query capability if migration only transforms stored records but not API contracts.

justification.inferredGoal: Remove the standalone Media surface from the core resource catalog.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep deprecated Media StructureDefinition and Media search parameters in the R6 base package for compatibility.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The codegen and REST-surface break follows directly from removing the base resource. If retiring `Media` is accepted as a consolidation goal, removing its generated classes, resourceType enum entry, endpoint, and search parameters is a coherent consequence. A compatibility surface was possible, but ordinary server adapters or conversion tooling are mitigations rather than a less-breaking base R6 design.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would have retained the deprecated `Media` StructureDefinition and its search parameter definitions so R6 generators could still emit legacy types and route/search metadata. That would protect R4 clients during a transition, but it would also make the deprecated resource a continuing normative surface for servers and SDKs, preserving exactly the API area R6 appears to be retiring.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids generated-client and endpoint breaks, but forces R6 tooling and servers to carry legacy model and search semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 package index includes multiple Media-specific SearchParameter definitions.
R6 package index has no Media StructureDefinition or Media-specific search parameter family.
R6 DiagnosticReport key media/data references point to DocumentReference, not Media.

examples.examplesMd: A generated R4 client method such as `client.search({ resourceType: "Media", searchParams: { subject: "Patient/123" } })` has no direct R6 core endpoint or generated model target.

findings.narrativeMd: The absence of `Media` changes more than validation. Code generators normally emit one class per resource, resource-type enums, serializers, and search parameter constants from the package. Those artifacts disappear for `Media` in R6, so code that compiles cleanly against R4 definitions can fail to compile or route in R6 even before any data migration runs.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This finding is not counted as a separate hard instance break because the root validation break is covered by the identity finding. It is still critical at runtime: R4 Media APIs, `_include` patterns, search parameters, and resource-type dispatch have no same-named R6 target.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update SDK models, route tables, persistence partitions, search indexes, subscriptions, and authorization policies that refer to `Media`. If backward compatibility is required, implement an explicit R4 compatibility endpoint or adapter that translates to chosen R6 targets and documents any lossy fields.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The less disruptive alternative would have been a deprecated core resource or official compatibility adapter. That would keep codegen stable while giving implementers time to migrate, but it would preserve a resource the R6 model apparently no longer wants to expose.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The runtime surface disappears with the resource: R4 package metadata includes `Media` search parameters and generators would normally emit `Media` classes, enum cases, serializers, and route/search constants, while the R6 package has no corresponding family. This is a concrete API/codegen break for any implementation that exposed `/Media` or compiled against generated R4 models. If R6 intentionally retires the resource, removing the generated and REST surface is coherent, but the absence of an R6 compatibility period or computable transition artifact still deserves review for clients using public Media profiles.
keyEvidence: R4 .index.json includes StructureDefinition-Media.json and Media-specific SearchParameter files for status, based-on, identifier, modality, device, created, site, subject, operator, encounter, view, patient, and type.
R6 .index.json query returned no Media StructureDefinition or Media-specific SearchParameter family.
R6 DiagnosticReport.media.link targets DocumentReference, not Media.
Public code search found IG/profile examples based on Media, indicating plausible generated-model and endpoint consumers even though production deployment was not proven.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1 lowers the compatibility burden, but generated APIs and REST/search behavior are implementation-facing surfaces; the public-profile evidence prevents treating this as harmless low-maturity cleanup.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: generated model classes, resource-type switches, REST routes, search parameters, subscriptions, and persistence schemas referring to Media disappear or require adapters.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: The base less-breaking option is to retain a deprecated Media definition and its search parameters so R6 tooling can still generate legacy surfaces. That is effective for compatibility but expensive because it preserves the exact endpoint and search model that R6 appears to be retiring.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing Critical runtime assessment is directionally right for systems exposing Media, and the Partial alternative is fair; the fresh judgment gives more weight to low FMM and to the tradeoff of carrying a legacy API surface.

findings.title: Media.status event lifecycle does not map cleanly to candidate R6 status elements

oldState.summary: R4 `Media.status` is mandatory, modifier, and bound required to event-status.

binding.description: Codes identifying the lifecycle stage of an event.

semanticText.comment: Unknown does not represent "other" - one of the defined statuses must apply. Unknown is used when the authoring system is not sure what the current status is.

oldState.narrativeMd: `Media.status` used the Event pattern statuses: `preparation`, `in-progress`, `not-done`, `on-hold`, `stopped`, `completed`, `entered-in-error`, and `unknown`.

newState.summary: No R6 `Media.status` exists; candidate target status elements use different lifecycle domains.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: `DocumentReference.status` is required to document-reference-status (`current`, `superseded`, `entered-in-error`, `unknown`); `DocumentReference.docStatus` is composition/document lifecycle; `ImagingSelection.status` is available/entered-in-error/inactive/unknown. These are not the R4 event-status value set.

newState.narrativeMd: The likely replacement status fields describe document-reference validity, underlying document lifecycle, or imaging-selection availability, not the event lifecycle of media acquisition.

facts.newValue: no obvious single required-code equivalent in candidate target statuses

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Status mapping was assessed against likely replacement resources because no R6 `Media.status` exists. The mapping is necessarily inferred and use-case dependent.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Raw R4 Media already fails because the resource is removed. For transformed data, lifecycle semantics can still break: an R4 media-acquisition event that is `in-progress`, `not-done`, or `on-hold` cannot be represented by simply copying the code into `DocumentReference.status` or `ImagingSelection.status` under their required bindings.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrectly mapping a not-done or entered-in-error acquisition to a current/available document can cause consumers to treat unavailable or invalid media as clinically usable.

justification.inferredGoal: Align migrated media with document-reference or imaging-selection lifecycle semantics.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Preserve the R4 event-status field in a deprecated Media resource or as a native compatibility status in a base replacement model.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Moving media content into resources with their own lifecycle semantics is reasonable, and status is a modifier where confusing event status with document/reference availability can be unsafe. A less-breaking base design could preserve the old event-status value separately, but doing so inside replacement resources would create competing status fields with different meanings. ConceptMaps, extensions, or conversion guidance alone would be migration mitigations, not a fully backward-compatible base design.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The strongest base alternative is to keep deprecated `Media.status` unchanged on a retained `Media` resource, or to add an explicit native compatibility field for original media event status. That would keep old lifecycle values valid, but consumers would then need to reconcile old event states such as `not-done` or `on-hold` with R6 `DocumentReference.status` or `ImagingSelection.status`, increasing validation ambiguity and clinical interpretation risk.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old lifecycle state, but duplicates or conflicts with modifier status meanings on DocumentReference and ImagingSelection.

evidence.detail: R4 Media.status is 1..1, modifier, required-bound to event-status.
evidence.quote: preparation | in-progress | not-done | on-hold | stopped | completed | entered-in-error | unknown

evidence.detail: DocumentReference uses document-reference and document/composition status domains rather than event-status.
ImagingSelection.status is required-bound to available, entered-in-error, inactive, and unknown.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is illustrative only. An official extension or ConceptMap would be preferable to a local example URL.

findings.narrativeMd: `Media.status` is a modifier because some status codes, especially `entered-in-error`, change whether the resource should be treated as valid. Candidate R6 targets have different lifecycle concepts. A naive transformation that maps `completed` to `current` or `not-done` to `unknown` can make a process/event state look like a document availability state.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An untransformed R4 Media instance is invalid in R6 because Media is absent. A transformed instance can also become invalid if an old event-status code is copied into a required R6 status binding that does not contain it. Even when validation succeeds, behavior can change if consumers interpret `current` or `available` differently from R4 `completed`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Create a status mapping policy before bulk migration. Treat `entered-in-error` explicitly. For old states without exact R6 equivalents, either use an extension preserving the original event status, map to a conservative R6 status plus explanatory metadata, or route those records for manual review. Test every R4 event-status code.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The status-domain mismatch could have been reduced by an official ConceptMap or by retaining an event-status field on a compatibility profile. The alternative preserves meaning but requires more specification work and may duplicate lifecycle concepts already present in target resources.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review is especially important for `not-done`, `on-hold`, and `stopped`, where no candidate target status is obviously equivalent.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `Media.status` is a required modifier in R4 bound to event lifecycle states such as `preparation`, `in-progress`, `not-done`, `on-hold`, `stopped`, `completed`, `entered-in-error`, and `unknown`. The plausible R6 targets use different status domains: `DocumentReference.status` is about the reference/document lifecycle, while `ImagingSelection.status` is about availability of a DICOM selection. Copying or flattening event states can turn a not-done or on-hold acquisition into an available/current document-like object, so migration requires clinical/business rules rather than mechanical conversion.
keyEvidence: R4 Media.status: min 1, max 1, isModifier true, required binding to ValueSet/event-status.
R4 CodeSystem-event-status includes preparation, in-progress, not-done, on-hold, stopped, completed, entered-in-error, and unknown.
R6 DocumentReference.status is required-bound to document-reference-status concepts such as current, superseded, and entered-in-error.
R6 ImagingSelection.status is required-bound to available, entered-in-error, inactive, and unknown, and is defined as distinct from associated study/request/task status.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Low FMM reduces the assumption that many deployed systems depend on every status, but status is a modifier and can affect whether media should be treated as clinically usable; that keeps the concern above ordinary low-FMM churn.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: transformed records may lose or misstate original event lifecycle semantics, and some old status codes have no direct required-code counterpart in candidate R6 targets.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking design could retain deprecated `Media.status` or add an explicit original media event-status field in a base compatibility model. The tradeoff is real: it would create parallel lifecycle/status concepts that consumers must reconcile with DocumentReference or ImagingSelection status.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing High impact and Partial alternative are supported by the modifier status mismatch, though the fresh review frames the concern as lossy semantic migration rather than a standalone raw-instance break beyond resource removal.

findings.title: Media.content attachment requires structural remapping and may not round-trip losslessly

oldState.summary: R4 `Media.content` is a mandatory single Attachment directly on Media.

semanticText.definition: The actual content of the media - inline or by direct reference to the media source file.
semanticText.comment: Recommended content types include image/jpeg, image/png, image/tiff, video/mpeg, audio/mp4, and application/dicom.

oldState.narrativeMd: `Media.content` is the required payload/reference for the media recording.

newState.summary: No R6 `Media.content` exists; DocumentReference carries attachments under repeating `content.attachment`.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 `DocumentReference.content` is 1..* and each repetition has a mandatory `content.attachment`. Its comment says multiple repetitions must represent the same document in different format or attachment metadata, not different versions.

facts.newValue: one or more DocumentReference.content backbone repetitions, each with an Attachment

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The attachment itself is a strong structural match, and R6 DiagnosticReport media links now target DocumentReference. However, DocumentReference is not a formally identified one-to-one successor for all Media uses in the supplied inputs.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Attachment bytes or URLs can often be carried forward, but the surrounding resource semantics and cardinality differ. R6 DocumentReference can contain multiple content representations and profile metadata that have no direct single `Media.content` home. Conversely, a single R4 Media attachment does not by itself supply all metadata a target DocumentReference may need for high-quality indexing.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect attachment migration can break access to clinical images, audio, or video, or can mix alternate formats/versions incorrectly.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent media payloads using the broader document/content reference pattern.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the old single Media.content attachment shape in a deprecated Media resource or a native R6 compatibility container.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Using `DocumentReference.content.attachment` for document-like media payloads is a reasonable R6 design direction and can carry many old Attachment values. The less-breaking option of retaining the old direct attachment shape would reduce migration work, but it would preserve a parallel representation that overlaps with the richer DocumentReference content backbone. Because that overlap is material, the structural break is probably justified, though not proven by local rationale.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A backward-compatible base design could have retained deprecated `Media.content` or added a native compatibility container that accepts the original single Attachment semantics. This would preserve most old payloads directly. Its cost is long-term duplication with `DocumentReference.content`, especially around repeated content entries, alternate representations, version handling, and whether generic audio/video/photo content is document-like.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves the payload shape, but duplicates the DocumentReference content model and leaves ambiguous rules for alternate formats and versions.

evidence.detail: R4 Media.content is 1..1 Attachment and isSummary true.
R6 DocumentReference.content is 1..* and content.attachment is 1..1 Attachment.
R6 DiagnosticReport media links reference DocumentReference.

examples.examplesMd: This illustrates a likely content-preserving transform, not a complete lossless migration. Status, type/category, encounter/context, author/operator, and technical metadata still need mapping.

findings.narrativeMd: The most obvious data-preserving move is to put the old `Media.content` attachment into `DocumentReference.content.attachment`. That saves the bytes or URL but changes the container from an event-like media recording to a document/content reference. Implementers must also decide whether alternate encodings, thumbnails, or versions become multiple `DocumentReference.content` entries, multiple DocumentReferences, or extensions.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Untransformed R4 is invalid because `Media` is absent. A transformed R6 DocumentReference with multiple content entries or content profiles is not cleanly representable as a single R4 `Media.content` Attachment. A one-attachment R4 Media can usually be represented in R6 DocumentReference, but validation depends on also supplying required target status/content structure.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map attachment data/url/contentType/hash/size/title/creation carefully. Decide whether `Media.issued` maps to `DocumentReference.date`, whether capture time maps to `DocumentReference.period` or attachment metadata, and how to represent alternate formats versus versions. Include tests for inline data, URL-only attachments, DICOM content, and multiple-format target representations.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A direct optional compatibility extension on DocumentReference could preserve original Media identity and content semantics. That is less breaking for round trip but requires consumers to understand the extension and still does not reintroduce `/Media` APIs.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The attachment payload has a straightforward R6 home for common cases: a single R4 `Media.content` Attachment can be placed in one `DocumentReference.content.attachment`. The migration is still breaking because the containing resource and content repetition semantics change, and round-tripping alternate formats or versions may require policy decisions. However, R6 `DocumentReference` explicitly covers photo, video, and audio recordings and its content backbone is designed for referenced serialized objects, so the structural change appears proportionate once the resource consolidation goal is accepted.
keyEvidence: R4 Media.content: min 1, max 1, type Attachment, actual content inline or by direct reference.
R6 DocumentReference.content: min 1, max *, with content.attachment min 1 max 1 Attachment.
R6 DocumentReference.content definition says repeated content entries must represent the same document in different format or attachment metadata.
R6 DiagnosticReport.media.link points to DocumentReference.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1/trial-use softens the stability concern; the attachment itself is not lost for typical single-content instances, so the remaining burden is migration policy and API change rather than a high-stability violation.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: the payload can usually be carried forward, but the old single event-like Media container does not round-trip cleanly against DocumentReference's repeated content/backbone semantics.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Retaining deprecated `Media.content` or adding a native single-attachment compatibility container would preserve the old shape, but it would duplicate the richer DocumentReference content model and leave ambiguous rules for alternate representations and versions.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report correctly identifies real migration work and a Partial alternative, but its High impact overstates the content-specific risk because the Attachment has a direct R6 representation.

findings.title: Media-specific acquisition and technical metadata have no single R6 replacement home

affectedLocation.oldPath: Media.type, Media.modality, Media.view, Media.bodySite, Media.deviceName, Media.device, Media.height, Media.width, Media.frames, Media.duration
affectedLocation.newPath: DocumentReference and ImagingSelection candidate fields, extensions, or external metadata

oldState.summary: R4 Media has local fields for acquisition category, modality, view, body site, device, dimensions, frame count, and duration.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `Media` directly models both the media payload and many capture-specific details: `type`, `modality`, `view`, `bodySite`, `deviceName`, `device`, `height`, `width`, `frames`, and `duration`.

newState.summary: No R6 Media fields exist; candidate replacements distribute or omit these concepts.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 `DocumentReference` has fields such as `modality`, `bodyStructure`, `type`, `category`, `period`, `date`, and `author`, but not direct `height`, `width`, `frames`, `duration`, `view`, or `deviceName` fields. R6 `ImagingSelection` has DICOM-oriented selection fields, body site, modality, performer, and selected frames, but does not carry a generic media attachment payload.

facts.newValue: no single R6 Media path; partial candidate homes vary by target resource

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Some concepts have clear partial matches, but the replacement is split by use case and cannot be inferred mechanically from the Media StructureDefinition alone.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Existing R4 data that relies on Media's technical fields can lose queryability or meaning if migrated only to a basic DocumentReference. R6 imaging resources may preserve some DICOM-specific details but are not a generic photo/audio/video replacement.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Image dimensions, frame counts, body site, and device context can affect display, interpretation, audit, and downstream image processing.

justification.inferredGoal: Move generic content to DocumentReference and imaging-specific selection metadata to imaging resources.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain deprecated Media fields or add native optional base metadata fields for common legacy dimensions, duration, frame, view, and device facts.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Splitting generic content from DICOM-oriented imaging selection is a reasonable goal, but the local R6 evidence does not show a complete native home for common non-DICOM media metadata such as dimensions, frame count, duration, view, and device name. A less-breaking base design could preserve many of those facts without relying only on extensions or local conversion rules. Because that alternative would still be incomplete for specialized imaging and would duplicate metadata concepts, it is partial, but the loss of first-class metadata is not clearly justified from the supplied inputs.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best base alternative would keep these elements on deprecated `Media`, or add optional native compatibility metadata to the relevant replacement resource model for common legacy media facts. That would preserve common R4 photo/audio/video metadata and reduce semantic loss. The tradeoff is that `DocumentReference` and `ImagingSelection` would accumulate generic-media fields that may not fit their primary semantics, while deprecated representations could persist indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Improves fidelity for generic media, but adds media-specific clutter and duplicated metadata beside document and DICOM-oriented models.

evidence.detail: R4 Media has direct local elements for media dimensions, frame count, duration, view, device name, and observing device.
DocumentReference has partial metadata homes but no direct height/width/frames/duration/view/deviceName fields.
ImagingSelection has DICOM-oriented selection fields including selected frames, modality, body site, and performer.

examples.examplesMd: The old fragment's duration, dimensions, and frame count have no obvious native fields in a simple DocumentReference transform.

findings.narrativeMd: R4 `Media` combined payload, capture event, and technical media metadata. In R6, likely target resources split those concerns. A generic DocumentReference migration may preserve the attachment but drop display-critical or acquisition-critical metadata unless extensions or specialized imaging resources are used.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: The raw R4 instance is invalid in R6. A transformed instance can validate while being semantically incomplete if these fields are omitted. R6 DICOM-oriented ImagingSelection details cannot always be represented in R4 Media either, especially selected instances, regions, or DICOM UIDs beyond the coarse R4 fields.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Create separate mapping rules for generic photos, scanned documents, audio/video recordings, and DICOM-derived media. Preserve dimensions and duration either in standardized extensions, attachment metadata when appropriate, or linked imaging resources. Test migration with still images, multi-frame images, videos, audio, scanned documents, and DICOM content.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible path would have kept these fields in a deprecated Media or provided a standardized extension set on replacement resources. The tradeoff is preserving a generic media model alongside more specialized document and imaging models.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The appropriate target for `Media.view` and `Media.deviceName` is especially unclear without official migration guidance.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `Media` carried first-class acquisition and technical facts such as dimensions, frame count, duration, view, device name, and observing device. R6 `DocumentReference` can preserve the payload and some descriptive metadata, and `ImagingSelection` has DICOM-oriented selection fields, but neither is a complete generic replacement for non-DICOM photo/audio/video metadata. This is a lossy migration risk for display, audit, and downstream processing, especially for IGs that profile Media for endoscopy, pathology, or attached images.
keyEvidence: R4 Media has height, width, frames, duration, view, deviceName, and device elements; Media.frames warns that multi-frame rendering needs to know when more than one frame exists.
R6 DocumentReference has modality, bodyStructure, content.attachment, and author but no direct height, width, frames, duration, view, or deviceName fields.
R6 ImagingSelection is defined as a selection of DICOM SOP instances and includes DICOM study/series/instance fields plus selected frames/body site/modality.
Public profile search found Media-based endoscopy/pathology/attached-image profiles, suggesting these metadata are not purely hypothetical.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1 lowers the presumption of broad installed-base harm, but the affected data can be display- and interpretation-relevant and public profile evidence points to real implementation interest.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: common media acquisition and rendering metadata may have no first-class R6 target unless implementations use extensions or specialized imaging resources.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could retain deprecated Media metadata or add optional native metadata for dimensions, duration, frames, device, and view on an appropriate R6 content model. That would improve fidelity but would add generic-media clutter to DocumentReference or duplicate concepts beside DICOM-oriented resources.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing High impact is credible for metadata-heavy media, and the Partial alternative is plausible; the fresh review emphasizes that the concern is strongest for non-DICOM or display-sensitive media, not every Media instance.

findings.title: Subject, operator, order, encounter, and part-of references require use-case-specific target mapping

oldState.summary: R4 Media defines specific reference roles and target profiles for media subject, operator, order, larger event, and encounter.
oldState.narrativeMd: `Media.subject` includes Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Group, Device, Specimen, and Location. `Media.operator` includes Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, CareTeam, Patient, Device, and RelatedPerson. `Media.basedOn` is ServiceRequest or CarePlan, `Media.encounter` is Encounter, and `Media.partOf` can reference any Resource.

newState.summary: Candidate R6 targets use different roles and target sets.
newState.narrativeMd: DocumentReference is broader for subject but changes operator to author and encounter to context. ImagingSelection is more imaging-specific and excludes some old Media subject targets such as Location and PractitionerRole while adding others such as Procedure, Medication, and Substance.

facts.newValue: DocumentReference.subject allows Resource; ImagingSelection.subject uses a different explicit target list

facts.oldValue: person or device who generated the image
facts.newValue: DocumentReference.author or ImagingSelection.performer.actor, neither an exact role-name match
DocumentReference.related.target Reference(Resource) or ImagingSelection.derivedFrom Reference(ImagingStudy|DocumentReference), depending on semantics

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The paths were matched by role semantics, not by direct element identity. Because no R6 Media exists, target selection depends on whether the old resource represented a document-like artifact, an imaging selection, or another media use case.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Some old references map cleanly, but others change role semantics or target domains. For example, a `Location` subject can be represented by broad DocumentReference.subject but not by ImagingSelection.subject; an old operator may be an author in DocumentReference only if that is semantically true.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misplaced subject or performer references can affect search, audit, provenance, and clinical context.

justification.inferredGoal: Use target-resource-specific reference roles instead of a generic Media event model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the original Media reference-role fields in a deprecated resource or native base compatibility fields.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Using target-resource-specific reference roles is a reasonable R6 design goal: `DocumentReference`, `ImagingSelection`, and other targets should name references according to their own semantics. The less-breaking alternative would keep old role names and target lists, but that creates long-lived ambiguity about whether a participant is an author, performer, subject, context, related resource, or part of an acquisition event. That semantic cost makes the break probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A base-compatible path would retain `Media.subject`, `Media.operator`, `Media.basedOn`, `Media.partOf`, and `Media.encounter` on deprecated `Media`, or add native original-role fields in a compatibility model. This would preserve most old references, but it would also duplicate the replacement resources' own roles and could encourage valid-looking records whose role semantics are not equivalent.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old references, but duplicates role semantics and can validate references in fields whose R6 meaning is only approximate.

evidence.detail: R4 Media defines local reference elements for subject, operator, order, part-of, and encounter with specific target profiles.
DocumentReference has candidate but semantically different reference roles.
ImagingSelection has imaging-specific reference roles and target profiles.

examples.examplesMd: A Location subject is allowed by R4 Media. If the implementer chooses ImagingSelection as the target, that subject target is not in ImagingSelection.subject's listed target profiles; DocumentReference.subject is a better structural fit but may change the clinical meaning.

findings.narrativeMd: The removal of Media forces role interpretation. `subject`, `operator`, `encounter`, `basedOn`, and `partOf` are not just references; they encode why the media exists and how it is used. Candidate R6 resources have different names and target lists, so a generic field-to-field copy can create valid but misleading records.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Raw R4 Media is invalid in R6. During transformation, some references can become invalid if copied into a target field with narrower profiles, while others can validate but change query behavior. R6 target resources can also express relationships that have no exact R4 Media counterpart.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Define mapping by use case. For document-like media, map subject/context/author/basedOn/related to DocumentReference where semantics match. For DICOM imaging selections, use ImagingSelection fields and handle unsupported old target types manually. Preserve original role in extensions when the target role is only approximate.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A compatibility map could avoid most accidental misplacements, but a perfect backward-compatible alternative would have kept the original Media role names. That would conflict with using more specialized target-resource semantics.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The participant/reference roles do not copy one-for-one, but most have plausible R6 homes once the target resource is chosen: `DocumentReference.subject`, `context`, `author`, `basedOn`, and `related`, or `ImagingSelection.subject`, `performer.actor`, `basedOn`, and `derivedFrom`. The hard part is role semantics, not raw representability. For example, an operator is not always a document author, and `partOf` may need a more specific related/context relationship. That is real migration work, but retaining all old role names in base R6 would undermine the target resources' clearer semantics.
keyEvidence: R4 Media.subject targets Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Group, Device, Specimen, and Location; operator targets practitioner/organization/care team/patient/device/related person roles.
R4 Media.basedOn, partOf, and encounter encode order, parent event, and encounter context.
R6 DocumentReference has broad subject Resource, context for Encounter/Appointment/EpisodeOfCare, author, basedOn, and related.
R6 ImagingSelection has subject, performer.actor, basedOn, and derivedFrom, but with imaging-specific semantics.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1 softens the compatibility concern and there is no strong evidence that these role mappings are broadly production-critical; migration remains important for adopters but not disproportionate as a base-model change.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: reference targets are often representable, but original Media role semantics can be blurred or require case-by-case mapping.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Keeping the original Media reference-role fields in deprecated Media or adding native original-role fields would preserve old data, but it would duplicate and potentially conflict with DocumentReference and ImagingSelection role semantics.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing Medium impact and Partial alternative match the evidence; the break is mostly semantic mapping work with meaningful tradeoffs for a more compatible design.

findings.title: Media-specific type/modality/view terminology is absent or replaced by document and DICOM-oriented terminology

oldState.summary: R4 Media binds media classification and acquisition concepts to Media-specific value sets.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 `Media.type` is extensible to `ValueSet/media-type`, whose code system includes `image`, `video`, and `audio`. R4 also has `media-modality` and `media-view` value sets.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 has `Media.type` for high-level image/video/audio, `Media.modality` for acquisition equipment/process, `Media.view` for projection, `Media.reasonCode`, and `Media.bodySite`.

newState.summary: R6 package has no `ValueSet-media-*` or `CodeSystem-media-*` files; candidate targets use different terminology.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R6 DocumentReference uses document type/category terminology and DICOM modality; ImagingSelection uses DICOM/image-reference terminology. Body site remains an example binding to `ValueSet/body-site` in candidate paths.

newState.narrativeMd: The old Media-specific codes are not present as same-named R6 terminology artifacts in the supplied package. Classification may need to be re-expressed as document type/category, DICOM modality, content type, or extensions.

facts.newValue: must be represented through target-specific terminology, MIME type, or extension
no CodeSystem-media* or ValueSet-media* files found in R6 package

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old terminology was compared to same-named package artifacts and candidate replacement bindings, but expansions and official maps were not available.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Most old Media terminology bindings were extensible or example, so the terminology change is not by itself a hard validation break after choosing a target. It is still semantically important because image/video/audio classification, modality, and view may drive search, display, routing, and analytics.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misclassified media can affect discoverability and display selection, but the supplied evidence does not show a direct required-binding clinical safety break except for status, which is covered separately.

justification.inferredGoal: Replace Media-specific terminology with resource-specific document, DICOM, and general body-site terminology.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain legacy media-type, media-modality, and media-view terminology artifacts and explicitly allow or cross-reference old codings in R6 target bindings.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Replacing generic media terminology with document and DICOM-oriented terminology is a reasonable direction, but the terminology-specific disruption appears avoidable. Unlike retaining a whole resource, keeping deprecated CodeSystems/ValueSets or broadening R6 CodeableConcept guidance to preserve old codings has relatively modest long-term cost. The local evidence does not show why image/video/audio, modality, or view codings had to lose a base-recognized legacy path.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base terminology design could keep the old media terminology artifacts as deprecated or legacy, and state where old media codings may be carried alongside preferred document or DICOM codings. This is more than ordinary conversion guidance because it preserves the legacy terminology as part of the R6 base package. It would not solve the root `Media` removal, but it would preserve the classification facts with little structural duplication.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Low structural cost; main tradeoff is mixed legacy and target-specific codings that complicate search and analytics.

evidence.locator: Media.type, Media.modality, Media.view, Media.reasonCode, Media.bodySite bindings
evidence.detail: R4 Media has local terminology bindings for type, modality, view, reason, and body site.
R4 media-type code system contains image, video, and audio.
No same-named R6 media terminology files were found.
Candidate replacement resources use document, DICOM, image-reference, and body-site terminology rather than Media-specific bindings.

examples.examplesMd: The old `audio` classification may be inferable from MIME type in a target resource, but it is not a same-path, same-binding migration.

findings.narrativeMd: R4 Media has simple, media-specific classification terminology. In R6 candidate targets, classification is more context-specific: document type/category, DICOM modality, image-reference type, and MIME type may all be relevant. This can improve domain precision but makes automated migration of old media categories ambiguous.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: The old extensible/example media bindings are not the primary hard validation issue. The risk is semantic and operational: migrated records may validate while losing the original image/video/audio or modality/view classification used by applications and search indexes. Required status terminology is covered in the separate status finding.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Retain original codings where target CodeableConcept fields permit them, add target-specific codings for document or imaging workflows, and use MIME type as supporting but not sole evidence. Build ConceptMaps or local mapping tables for `media-type`, `media-modality`, and `media-view` before migration.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The less disruptive path would provide official ConceptMaps and possibly preserve media-specific value sets as legacy terminology. That would ease migration while allowing new target resources to use more precise terminology.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Terminology expansion was not performed, and external DICOM/LOINC/SNOMED bindings may materially affect production mappings.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The terminology change is not a meaningful standalone compatibility problem. R4 `Media.type` was extensible, while `Media.modality` and `Media.view` were example bindings, so the absence of same-named R6 media terminology in the local core package does not by itself reject old codes after a target resource is selected. R6 target resources use more specific document, DICOM, body-site, and MIME-type classification mechanisms. Retaining legacy media terminology could help migration, but the required compatibility problem is already the resource/API removal, not a separate required-binding break.
keyEvidence: R4 Media.type is CodeableConcept with extensible binding to ValueSet/media-type.
R4 CodeSystem-media-type contains only image, video, and audio.
R4 Media.modality and Media.view use example bindings.
No CodeSystem-media*.json or ValueSet-media*.json files were found in the R6 ballot4 core package.
R6 DocumentReference.type/category/modality and ImagingSelection.category/code/modality provide flexible or domain-specific classification targets.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1 further reduces the need to preserve low-maturity legacy terminology in the R6 core package when the old bindings were mostly non-required and replacement resources provide other classification mechanisms.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: semantic/documentation: old classification codes may need mapping for search/display consistency, but this is not an old-valid/new-invalid terminology break by itself.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Keeping deprecated media terminology artifacts or cross-referencing old codings in R6 would be low structural cost, but it would not solve the root Media removal and could mix legacy generic media codes with more precise document/DICOM classifications. Helpful migration guidance is enough here.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree: the existing report's Medium impact and Yes alternative overstate this finding as a base compatibility issue; the old bindings were not mostly required, so this is best treated as migration guidance rather than a problem.

findings.title: Media.created[x] and Media.issued timing semantics need explicit target mapping

oldState.summary: R4 Media distinguishes collection time from availability time.
oldState.narrativeMd: `Media.created[x]` is when the media was collected and can be a `dateTime` or `Period`. `Media.issued` is when this version was made available, typically after review.

newState.summary: Candidate replacement resources use different timing concepts.
newState.narrativeMd: `DocumentReference.period` is the time of service being documented and `DocumentReference.date` is when the document reference was created. `ImagingSelection.issued` is when the imaging selection was created. None is a same-name replacement for both collection and availability timing.

facts.newValue: candidate DocumentReference.period or attachment metadata; no R6 Media path
candidate DocumentReference.date or ImagingSelection.issued, depending on target semantics

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Timing fields were matched by definitions. The target concepts are close but not identical.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Timing fields often drive sorting, version tracking, and clinical context. A valid migration can still change meaning if capture time is placed in document-reference creation time or vice versa.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Wrong timestamps can affect chronology and audit, especially for recordings spanning a period.

justification.inferredGoal: Use target-resource timing fields rather than Media-specific event timing.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Define native base timing compatibility for original capture period/time and reviewed-availability instant, or retain the old fields on deprecated Media.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Using target-resource timing fields is a reasonable goal, and `DocumentReference.period`, `DocumentReference.date`, and `ImagingSelection.issued` cover nearby concepts. However, the R4 distinction between collection time and reviewed availability time is important and could have been preserved more explicitly in base definitions for common cases. Because the available less-breaking design would still need semantic policy decisions and may duplicate existing timing fields, it is partial, but the current level of ambiguity is not clearly justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could retain `Media.created[x]` and `Media.issued` on deprecated `Media`, or define native compatibility timing elements/aliases that distinguish capture time or period from reference creation and availability/review time. This would preserve many R4 timing semantics. The tradeoff is overlap with existing target fields, plus inconsistent interpretation if implementers treat capture, service period, reference creation, and availability as interchangeable.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Covers common timing cases, but may duplicate target timing concepts and still needs policy for exact event semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 Media has separate collection and issued/availability timing.
DocumentReference period and date definitions describe service time and reference creation time.
ImagingSelection.issued is when the imaging selection was created.

examples.examplesMd: The old period describes recording collection; the issued instant describes when the media version became available. A target DocumentReference needs a policy for `period` versus `date` and any attachment creation metadata.

findings.narrativeMd: Timing is not just a datatype conversion. R4 separates when media was collected from when it was issued. Candidate R6 targets use document/service/reference/selection timing concepts that can overlap but are not equivalent. Incorrect mapping can reorder clinical events or obscure review/availability timing.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Raw R4 Media is invalid in R6. After transformation, date values may validate but represent a different business event. R6 target records with multiple timing concepts may not be reducible to the two old Media timing fields without policy decisions.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Document a timing policy before migration. For DocumentReference, consider mapping recording period to `period` and availability/reference creation to `date` only when definitions match the business event; otherwise preserve source timing in extensions or Provenance. Test instantaneous captures and duration-based recordings separately.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: An official mapping could have made this mostly backward compatible by defining exact timing semantics. Without that, implementations must choose locally and risk inconsistent conversions.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 separates collection time (`created[x]`, dateTime or Period) from availability/review time (`issued`, instant). R6 candidate targets have nearby but not identical fields: `DocumentReference.period` is the time of service being documented, `DocumentReference.date` is when the reference was created, and `ImagingSelection.issued` is when the selection was created. A mechanical copy can change chronology or availability meaning, so migration rules are needed. Still, common cases can be represented well enough, and adding duplicate base timing aliases would create overlapping interpretations.
keyEvidence: R4 Media.created[x]: dateTime or Period, defined as when the media was collected.
R4 Media.issued: instant, defined as when this version was made available, typically after review.
R6 DocumentReference.period: time of service being documented; DocumentReference.date: when the document reference was created.
R6 ImagingSelection.issued: date and time the imaging selection was created.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 1 softens the stability concern; this is important for adopters with chronology-sensitive media, but it is not enough on its own to require preserving the old timing fields in base R6.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: capture time, service/documentation time, reference creation time, and availability/review time can be conflated without explicit migration policy.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking design could retain deprecated `created[x]` and `issued` on Media or add native compatibility timing fields. That would preserve semantics but duplicate existing target timing concepts and still require policy for exact event meanings.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing Medium impact and Partial alternative are reasonable; the fresh review judges the burden proportionate because nearby R6 timing fields cover many common cases.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: No local R4 Media-specific invariants beyond common `ele-1`/extension constraints were found. Because R6 has no Media StructureDefinition, no R6 Media-local constraints could be compared; inherited base constraints are out of scope.
The R4 Media StructureDefinition did not define local slicing on Media elements. The removal of the resource is captured separately rather than as a slicing change.
No local fixed, pattern, or default value constraints were identified on R4 Media elements. The R6 absence of Media means there is no corresponding local fixed/pattern/default delta.
No Media-local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex constraints were identified apart from datatype choices such as `positiveInt` and `decimal`, whose datatype-level changes are out of scope.

R4 `Media.status` and inherited `implicitRules`/`modifierExtension` are modifiers. Candidate R6 resources also have modifier status elements, but there is no R6 Media element-by-element modifier-flag comparison to perform.
Most R4 Media business elements are marked summary. With no R6 Media counterpart, summary flag changes cannot be assessed locally except as part of the overall resource removal.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: DocumentReference can carry the old Attachment payload in a richer content container
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: This is not a non-breaking change to `Media` itself because `Media` is removed. It is a notable migration opportunity: R6 `DocumentReference.content.attachment` can preserve many old `Media.content` Attachment values.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Do not assume this is lossless. The target content repetitions represent alternate formats/metadata for the same document, not arbitrary multiple Media resources or versions.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: ImagingSelection offers richer DICOM-oriented selection metadata for some old imaging media
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: This is a candidate improvement for DICOM imaging workflows, not a direct replacement that preserves all R4 Media content.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Use ImagingSelection when the old Media represents selected DICOM instances/frames/regions. Generic photos, audio, video, and scanned documents usually need a different target such as DocumentReference.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Likely target for many R4 Media attachments and the target of R6 `DiagnosticReport.media.link`; needs its own full R4-to-R6 assessment and migration guidance.
Likely target for some DICOM imaging selection use cases that previously used Media-like references or metadata.
R4 `DiagnosticReport.media.link` targets Media, while R6 targets DocumentReference. That change belongs to the DiagnosticReport assessment but is important for Media migration planning.
Inherited base-artifact changes are explicitly out of scope for this Media report and should be handled by the relevant base artifact reports.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Because no R6 `Media` StructureDefinition exists, the analysis cannot perform a normal element-by-element same-artifact diff. Element-level findings are therefore framed as removal and migration risks rather than direct R6 Media deltas.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Official R6 migration notes, a retirement notice, or a canonical cross-version StructureMap/ConceptMap for Media would resolve most ambiguity.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4-to-R6 diff or Jira/change-note rationale was included in the local inputs.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Reviewing HL7 change proposals, ballot reconciliation notes, and narrative specification history would improve judgement about justification and intended alternatives.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Terminology conclusions are based on bindings and local code system/value set files, not live expansions or external terminology-server comparisons.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Compare expanded value sets and any official ConceptMaps for event-status, document-reference-status, imagingselection-status, media-type, media-modality, DICOM modality, and document type/category bindings.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The R6 package is a ballot build marked not for publication in package metadata. Final R6 content may differ.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Re-run the assessment against the final published R6 core package.

crossArtifactPatternsToCheck: R4 references to Media replaced by R6 references to DocumentReference
Retired resourceType values missing from R6 CodeSystem/StructureDefinition indexes
Event-status resources migrated to document or availability status domains
